items.title: Captain Price Actor Sends Message to Fans as Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 Campaign Praise Rolls in
items.description: Barry Sloane, the actor behind Call of Duty's Captain Price, has shared a message with fans as praise for Modern Warfare 4's campaign rolls in.
items.author: Michael Cripe
items.content:
Barry Sloane, the actor behind Call of Duty's Captain Price, has shared a message with fans as praise for Modern Warfare 4's campaign rolls in.

Early reactions to Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4's story mode have filled social media feeds in the first 24 hours since early access players dived in – and most of them seem to be quite positive. Fans online have called it one of the more "brutal" and "intense" campaigns the series has ever seen, with many going as far as to say it holds its own against classic stories featured in games like the original Modern Warfare 2 and Black Ops.

It appears to be a winner for publisher Activision and developer Infinity Ward that critics like, too. While Steam reviews paint a "Very Positive" picture, IGN awarded this year's set of story missions an 8/10. Our reviewer said the Modern Warfare 4 campaign made them "feel something for the series again," adding that it managed to send the reboot saga series out "on a high note."

"The MW4 campaign was a 10/10 for me, they made a good story and ended it," one recent Steam review said. "Damn near almost cried at the end LOL."

As reviews continue to trickle in, many have taken the time to praise Sloane's work as Captain Price, specifically. The star behind Activision's most recent incarnation of the Task Force 141 leader took to social media to respond to the "kind words" he's received.

"Thank you for all the kind words," he said. "I see them. I read them. And I am grateful."

As Infinity Ward sought to end this Modern Warfare storyline with the 2026 Call of Duty game, it should come as no surprise to see that the developers took big swings in its story. With that said, full-on, untagged Modern Warfare 4 campaign spoilers have already started to show up across feeds, too. There's not much Activision can do about that, but Sloane used his message as an opportunity to ask fans to keep unfiltered reactions to themselves, at least for now.

"Remember," he continued, "let's allow people to enjoy the game in their own time. No spoilers. Bravo 6 – Dark."

Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4's campaign is out now for early access players. Its DMZ mode will drop Tuesday, October 20, with the full release set to follow Friday, October 23, for PC, Nintendo Switch 2, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X/S. For a full debrief on the events of the FPS franchise's latest story mode, click here. You can also check out the full breakdown of release times here.

items.title: We Sat Down with D&D Game Designer James Wyatt to Talk Dungeons & Dragons: World of Warcraft
items.description: At New York Comic Con, I got a chance to sit down with Wizards of the Coast Principal Game Designer James Wyatt to talk about the first Universes Beyond expansion for D&D.
items.author: Jacqueline Thomas
items.content:
Dungeons & Dragons: World of Warcraft is less than a month away, and it already looks like it's going to be a massive expansion to the tabletop game. But there are still a lot of questions about whether this new expansion is going to lean more towards the combat-oriented approach of the MMO or just be a traditional D&D game on Azeroth.

At New York Comic Con, I got a chance to sit down with Wizards of the Coast principal game designer James Wyatt to talk about the first Universes Beyond expansion for D&D. From how he was talking about the expansion, it really does sound more like a D&D game taking place on Azeroth than trying to shove WoW's complicated mechanics and combat focus on the TTRPG.

IGN: I know that there are a lot of people who play both WoW and D&D, and I've heard some WoW players say that this is going to get them into D&D. Does the Expansion have a good on-ramp for those players?

James Wyatt: That is not its purpose, but I think it is a fantastic on-ramp in terms of someone who's a WoW player. Sitting down to make a D&D character, you're like, "Okay, what's a Tiefling? What's a Dragonborn? And what do these classes mean?" Whereas if you have that foundation of here's the WoW species, here's the WoW classes, you know the kind of character you want to make right away. This can help you steer and make those choices as a new player. We also have a very brief introductory "What is D&D?" just in case you don't know or for people who aren't familiar with it. And we steer you to D&D Beyond in particular as a place to find resources to help you get started.

So yeah, we took this down for a playtest at Blizzard last fall in the early stages, and Blizzard employees who had signed up, they signed up blind for a playtest of something. They didn't know what.

And so some of them were like, "Woo, D&D. Yes, I love D&D." And others are like, "Okay, I've never played it before. How does this go?" And I always love playing with new players because they don't know what they're supposed to do. So they are more willing to try anything they can imagine, which to my mind is really what the game is all about.

I was just telling the story of the guy who was playing the Forsaken Warlock who decided that, because he had no lower jaw, he couldn't properly cast spells. So his first spell backfired and knocked him down the stairs. And so then he tore off his own arm and threw it at the monster.

And, awesome! That's Dungeons & Dragons in a nutshell. It's not "What buttons do I have to press?" It's "What can I imagine and how do I do that? What does it look like?"

IGN: Yeah. Speaking of the combat, I know that there's a selection of dungeons that have been poured into the game, but obviously there are just too many dungeons in World of Warcraft to bring all of them over. So why did you pick the dungeons that you picked?

Wyatt: There were a couple of factors that went into that. One of them is that we started with this section on conflicts of Azeroth, which outlines the six conflicts that really have been the driving forces behind most of the expansions of WoW and talk about how they shape the world, and how you might bring them into a campaign.

All of the dungeons, I think, tie into these themes. That was one of the things that we used as a selection criteria is, does it reflect the themes of the conflicts that we're trying to emphasize here? So that was one. I was looking at popularity ranking on some wiki as another factor, just trying to get at what Dungeons people love and what's resonant for them. We started with a much larger list, made it smaller. So then it was what can we do in the space that we have and what works for the various level ranges of characters and that sort of thing.

IGN: There are some people who are probably going to want to see more of the raids. I think the only raid that I saw on the list was Onyxia's Lair, I might be mistaken. But will people be able to create their own Icecrown Citadel?

Wyatt: Icecrown Citadel, we are doing as a digital download adventure. We have a separate map pack that has five double-sided poster maps that are the boss fights from Icecrown Citadel. And that comes with a code for a digital download of the Icecrown Citadel adventure. So you can play through that. But I ran Blackfathom Deeps 20 years ago. It was just downloading the map from the internet and making up stats for Nagas at the time. And so using the tools in this book, you can absolutely adapt any dungeon you want to.

IGN: I saw some people concerned that this will be too focused on combat and having prescriptive dungeons. What would you say to that?

Wyatt: I think that's kind of the opposite of what we were going for, because the beauty of D&D is that when you walk into Shadowfang Keep, you can talk to anybody you meet, you can interact with anything you can see. And so the possibilities just open up tremendously over what a developer can program into any game, no matter how much care they're putting into it, because you have a DM at the table who can improvise and decide what happens.

So the dungeons that are presented here are given a pretty light touch and it's sort of like, okay, here's the dungeon map, here's the pins in the map that mark the bosses that we know you're going to encounter at some point. And what happens in between is largely a matter of improv and that you can roll on tables to generate encounters if you want a combat encounter, but you can also do something where you're exploring the environment in a way that you can't necessarily do in the MMO.

IGN: I take it that even the adventure hooks that you have open on that page there of Dire Maul, I'm sure people can create their own adventure hooks and assign their own reputation rewards and everything like that.

Wyatt: Yeah.

IGN: So this is for people who are familiar with Dungeons & Dragons at large. This is more of a guideline of how to play a game within World of Warcraft than anything else.

Wyatt: Yes, exactly. It is a great big toolbox. I mean, that's how I describe most of the books that I work on. I don't write a lot of adventure products. I do a lot of source books, and really there's that sense of we've got character options, we've got monsters, we've got dungeons you can explore. We've got guidelines for crafting your own campaign, and we've got just a big blank slate for you to play with.

IGN: World of Warcraft's obviously an evolving game that never really sits in one place. This goes up to the beginning of Midnight. Obviously, there's going to be more stories that come out over time. Are there going to be supplemental products or will it just be like, we gave you the tools, you know the story, kind of do your own thing with it?

Wyatt: Who knows? Okay, I keep saying that if I get to do another World of Warcraft book, I might postpone my retirement a little bit in order to work on it because I had so much fun working on this, loved it so much. And that depends entirely on my relationship with Blizzard and how things go from here, but I would love to do more.

And honestly, the book doesn't spend as much time on the War Within and Midnight as it could have. There's almost nothing about Xal'atath in here. Would've loved to give her a stat block, but she didn't sort of make the cut. And I'm not sure we could give her a stat block.

IGN: She does play into that Old Gods and the Void conflict pretty heavily.

Wyatt: Yeah. There's absolutely more we can do even with the story that exists now, as well as future stories. And I'm keeping a list that will be my outline as soon as I get the go-ahead and start working in another book if that ever happens. But for now, absolutely, if those are the next expansion is all about, give me something that they might focus on.

IGN: The next expansion is going to be The Last Titan, so I assume it's going to be about the Titans.

Wyatt: Right. Well, we can tell you a little bit about the Titans in here somewhere, beginning of chapter five. And honestly, my expectation is that anybody using this book is also going to spend a lot of time on the wikis because that information is there.

So yeah, we've got lots of resources for making a character that probably is not going to change significantly. I mean, the next time they give us a new class, it would be fun to do that in another D&D book.

IGN: Tell me a little bit about working the Devourer Demon Hunter into the book.

Wyatt: Pretty much as soon as I got access to the Midnight beta, I went and made a Devourer and started playing around with it and was reading what was, again, on the wikis about it. And so we already had the Demon Hunter set up with Havoc and Vengeance and just added some more spells and some direction about how to steer your Demon Hunter in that spec. They've got their own column of spells here with all the consuming soul stuff.

IGN: How did you work the WoW classes into D&D without kind of putting a wrench in the way classes traditionally work in Dungeons & Dragons?

Wyatt: The word I keep using is, rather than translation, paraphrase, that for each class I sat down and I looked at their abilities and their talent trees and all the things they can do. And I sort of cut off around level 60, I think. I don't remember now. I'd have to look at my spreadsheets. I have spreadsheets. Nobody told me that being a writer was going to involve so many spreadsheets.

And I looked for things that are already in D&D that we want to make sure to highlight in that specialization and that class, and look for opportunities to create new spells or feats or battle master maneuvers, or anything else to help evoke the most iconic flavor things.

Talents are really fiddly in WoW and D&D mechanics are not that fiddly. We don't deal with math at such a granular scale. And so again, evoking the flavor is more important to us than reproducing the mechanics in any way.

So each specialization has a selection of feats that would be good to help you do that. There is a fundamental difference though, that if you're playing a healing spec Paladin, you are a healer as opposed to a tank spec Paladin, who is a tank.

And in D&D, no matter what Paladin and subclass you choose and what feat you choose, you're both, you're a healer and a tank. And so you're not as narrowly defined by your role. So that remains true. And if you're playing a Priest, you can be wearing more than cloth armor because we couldn't easily take something away from the Cleric class to fit, and you're still casting the spells that you expect a WoW Priest to be casting.

So all of the classes I think are a little broader and give you more range of options while still helping you focus in on the role you're supposed to be playing.

IGN: I feel like in WoW stories, characters that embody those classes follow those rules anyways where it's more broad.

Wyatt: Yeah. They keep saying Anduin is a priest and there he is in plate armor with his sword.

IGN: Yeah, he is a special Priest, isn't he? So what about the mechanics for bosses? I know you described the Litch King Arthas fight, and I progressed that fight when it was current on Heroic 25, and it was hell, with mechanics like defile where you stand in it and it gets bigger. Is it as fraught or as dangerous, or is there kind of...

Wyatt: I mean, he's challenge rating 25, where D&D characters go up to level 20. So you know, it's going to be a tough fight. It's different because D&D combats are shorter in terms of the number of things you or the boss can do in the fight because they often take long enough even at three or four rounds compared to how quickly an MMO raid battle plays out, relatively speaking. So again, that idea of paraphrase rather than translation, we're trying to evoke the feeling of that fight without reproducing it exactly. But there's a lot going on here that will feel very familiar.

IGN: Could you go in and talk Arthas out of invading Azeroth with the Scourge or sneak in and steal the Helm of Domination and put it on yourself?

Wyatt: Theoretically. You can certainly try. And that's again the beauty of it, that you can talk to anybody.

IGN: Can you tell me a little bit more about the reputation system? Why did you think that was such an important thing to work into a Warcraft tabletop game?

Wyatt: So the renown system in the Dungeon Masters guide is sort of an optional rule. It's not something that we spend a lot of time with in the base game, but it is a great tool for giving factions in the world some kind of heft, a significant impact on characters' lives.

And so given particularly the importance of the Alliance and the Horde, and also the other factions in the game, I thought it would be pretty cool to use the renown system to reflect, to give characters some investment in those factions.

But fundamentally, you start caring about the welfare of the Horde if you're fighting for the Horde, and you're getting renown with the Horde, and you're getting benefits for that devotion to them.

So it's not load bearing. You can ignore it if you want to. The campaign that I'm playing in right now, it's weird because we've time traveled. We've gone back from Midnight to Classic. And so I'm not sure any of us are fully rooted in the world yet, but I'm really curious to see how that plays out over time.

I think we might have just gotten a renown reward in our last adventure, but I can't remember for sure. So yeah, it's fun. It's a way to root characters in the world and it's not essential. In the Icecrown Citadel adventure, we do a whole separate thing for your Renown with the Ashen Verdict, which goes up more quickly than you might expect Renown to go up in the core book.

But then you can get your rings improved by Armis the Penitent as your renown increases, and you're also collecting things that can make Shadowmourne and doing all of that in the context of working through the raid once rather than working through it repeatedly.

IGN: I think that's where the friction in my head is at. Because of all the time I've spent in WoW, I associate reputation with these massive grinds.

Wyatt: Yeah. That really is the key difference that even in Icecrown Citadel, I planned it out so that you get to, I think you get to 50 just about the time you kill the Lich King.

But it's like every single encounter in the Citadel, your renown increases by one or two, which is bigger than the rate we expect for most of these factions. The general idea is, and in the DMG, we even give you a conversion. If you don't want to track renown points, you can just use character level so that by the time you're 17th level, we assume you're exalted with your home faction.

IGN: On the time travel thing you mentioned earlier, the Chromie time. So for me, in the actual video game World of Warcraft, Chromie Time always felt kind of shoehorned in as "we need to get you to end game as fast as possible." And Chromie Time was just kind of the method to do that. Why Chromie Time?

Wyatt: Well, two things going on. The first is that Chromie wrote a little introduction to the book.

IGN: I love that.

Wyatt: Me too. Thank you. Where she's basically saying, "I put this book together to let you visit whatever part, basically to give you your own timeline to play in."

It's a way of expressly giving the reader permission to ignore Canon, fundamentally. That's all it is. The specific example of the campaign I'm playing in, that's our DM's concoction of, okay, the campaign I want to run is modern characters.

We started off in Silvermoon City. We've just repelled Xal'atath. We're eight characters. We've just helped support the effort to repel Xal'atath. And then suddenly the time stream changes and we're in a Silvermoon city that is run by dragons. And what has happened?

So we fight some dragons and get to safety and meet Chromie who says the time stream's gone amuck. I've got to send you back 20 years to before this to prevent whatever the Infinite Dragonflight has done to mess up the timestream. So that's the story we're playing, not essential to what's in the book.

IGN: Okay. So it's not some scheme for Chromie to become the Bronze Aspect?

Wyatt: Who knows? Maybe in your campaign.

IGN: She deserves it.

Wyatt: It's true. She's also got little notes scattered throughout the book.

IGN: Oh yeah?

Wyatt: Not very many of them, but wherever we had space on a page, she wrote a little note. "All these King Gorducks, or is it King Gordock? Anyway, I think all Big Ogres would benefit from spending some time small."

IGN: I think they would. That's a great addition. My final question is about Forever. I know you mentioned that it came out too late to get added to the book in any meaningful way, but if somebody wanted to add the Skyborne race or add the new zones that were added in, which I think a lot of the new zones in Forever were kind of cut content that existed in vanilla anyways, like Mount Hyjal.

Wyatt: Right. Yeah. I remember seeing that big blank spot on the map because I was playing early on. Yeah. Adding a new Elven lineage is not super complicated. It might be fun for us to talk to Blizzard about maybe doing that in a D&D Beyond drop or something.

But anything else that they've added content-wise, I think the content that they're adding is very easy to just port into the D&D campaign you're playing. And again, you can do anything you want. You can go anywhere you want.

IGN: I have to ask: Would you rather play Forever or Retail?

Wyatt: I wish I had time to do both. Right now I really don't have time to do either. So I've been dabbling with forever just a little bit, but I'm anxious to... I haven't finished the Midnight storyline yet, I think. So I'm anxious to get back to that, too.

Nobody told me that being a writer was going to involve so many spreadsheets.

And I looked for things that are already in D&D that we want to make sure to highlight in that specialization and that class, and look for opportunities to create new spells or feats or battle master maneuvers, or anything else to help evoke the most iconic flavor things.

Talents are really fiddly in WoW and D&D mechanics are not that fiddly. We don't deal with math at such a granular scale. And so again, evoking the flavor is more important to us than reproducing the mechanics in any way.

So each specialization has a selection of feats that would be good to help you do that. There is a fundamental difference though, that if you're playing a healing spec Paladin, you are a healer as opposed to a tank spec Paladin, who is a tank.

And in D&D, no matter what Paladin and subclass you choose and what feat you choose, you're both, you're a healer and a tank. And so you're not as narrowly defined by your role. So that remains true. And if you're playing a Priest, you can be wearing more than cloth armor because we couldn't easily take something away from the Cleric class to fit, and you're still casting the spells that you expect a WoW Priest to be casting.

So all of the classes I think are a little broader and give you more range of options while still helping you focus in on the role you're supposed to be playing.

IGN: I feel like in WoW stories, characters that embody those classes follow those rules anyways where it's more broad.

Wyatt: Yeah. They keep saying Anduin is a priest and there he is in plate armor with his sword.

IGN: Yeah, he is a special Priest, isn't he? So what about the mechanics for bosses? I know you described the Litch King Arthas fight, and I progressed that fight when it was current on Heroic 25, and it was hell, with mechanics like defile where you stand in it and it gets bigger. Is it as fraught or as dangerous, or is there kind of...

Wyatt: I mean, he's challenge rating 25, where D&D characters go up to level 20. So you know, it's going to be a tough fight. It's different because D&D combats are shorter in terms of the number of things you or the boss can do in the fight because they often take long enough even at three or four rounds compared to how quickly an MMO raid battle plays out, relatively speaking. So again, that idea of paraphrase rather than translation, we're trying to evoke the feeling of that fight without reproducing it exactly. But there's a lot going on here that will feel very familiar.

IGN: Could you go in and talk Arthas out of invading Azeroth with the Scourge or sneak in and steal the Helm of Domination and put it on yourself?

Wyatt: Theoretically. You can certainly try. And that's again the beauty of it, that you can talk to anybody.

IGN: Can you tell me a little bit more about the reputation system? Why did you think that was such an important thing to work into a Warcraft tabletop game?

Wyatt: So the renown system in the Dungeon Masters guide is sort of an optional rule. It's not something that we spend a lot of time with in the base game, but it is a great tool for giving factions in the world some kind of heft, a significant impact on characters' lives.

And so given particularly the importance of the Alliance and the Horde, and also the other factions in the game, I thought it would be pretty cool to use the renown system to reflect, to give characters some investment in those factions.

But fundamentally, you start caring about the welfare of the Horde if you're fighting for the Horde, and you're getting renown with the Horde, and you're getting benefits for that devotion to them.

So it's not load bearing. You can ignore it if you want to. The campaign that I'm playing in right now, it's weird because we've time traveled. We've gone back from Midnight to Classic. And so I'm not sure any of us are fully rooted in the world yet, but I'm really curious to see how that plays out over time.

I think we might have just gotten a renown reward in our last adventure, but I can't remember for sure. So yeah, it's fun. It's a way to root characters in the world and it's not essential. In the Icecrown Citadel adventure, we do a whole separate thing for your Renown with the Ashen Verdict, which goes up more quickly than you might expect Renown to go up in the core book.

But then you can get your rings improved by Armis the Penitent as your renown increases, and you're also collecting things that can make Shadowmourne and doing all of that in the context of working through the raid once rather than working through it repeatedly.

IGN: I think that's where the friction in my head is at. Because of all the time I've spent in WoW, I associate reputation with these massive grinds.

Wyatt: Yeah. That really is the key difference that even in Icecrown Citadel, I planned it out so that you get to, I think you get to 50 just about the time you kill the Lich King.

But it's like every single encounter in the Citadel, your renown increases by one or two, which is bigger than the rate we expect for most of these factions. The general idea is, and in the DMG, we even give you a conversion. If you don't want to track renown points, you can just use character level so that by the time you're 17th level, we assume you're exalted with your home faction.

IGN: On the time travel thing you mentioned earlier, the Chromie time. So for me, in the actual video game World of Warcraft, Chromie Time always felt kind of shoehorned in as "we need to get you to end game as fast as possible." And Chromie Time was just kind of the method to do that. Why Chromie Time?

Wyatt: Well, two things going on. The first is that Chromie wrote a little introduction to the book.

IGN: I love that.

Wyatt: Me too. Thank you. Where she's basically saying, "I put this book together to let you visit whatever part, basically to give you your own timeline to play in."

It's a way of expressly giving the reader permission to ignore Canon, fundamentally. That's all it is. The specific example of the campaign I'm playing in, that's our DM's concoction of, okay, the campaign I want to run is modern characters.

We started off in Silvermoon City. We've just repelled Xal'atath. We're eight characters. We've just helped support the effort to repel Xal'atath. And then suddenly the time stream changes and we're in a Silvermoon city that is run by dragons. And what has happened?

So we fight some dragons and get to safety and meet Chromie who says the time stream's gone amuck. I've got to send you back 20 years to before this to prevent whatever the Infinite Dragonflight has done to mess up the timestream. So that's the story we're playing, not essential to what's in the book.

IGN: Okay. So it's not some scheme for Chromie to become the Bronze Aspect?

Wyatt: Who knows? Maybe in your campaign.

IGN: She deserves it.

Wyatt: It's true. She's also got little notes scattered throughout the book.

IGN: Oh yeah?

Wyatt: Not very many of them, but wherever we had space on a page, she wrote a little note. "All these King Gorducks, or is it King Gordock? Anyway, I think all Big Ogres would benefit from spending some time small."

IGN: I think they would. That's a great addition. My final question is about Forever. I know you mentioned that it came out too late to get added to the book in any meaningful way, but if somebody wanted to add the Skyborne race or add the new zones that were added in, which I think a lot of the new zones in Forever were kind of cut content that existed in vanilla anyways, like Mount Hyjal.

Wyatt: Right. Yeah. I remember seeing that big blank spot on the map because I was playing early on. Yeah. Adding a new Elven lineage is not super complicated. It might be fun for us to talk to Blizzard about maybe doing that in a D&D Beyond drop or something.

But anything else that they've added content-wise, I think the content that they're adding is very easy to just port into the D&D campaign you're playing. And again, you can do anything you want. You can go anywhere you want.

IGN: I have to ask: Would you rather play Forever or Retail?

Wyatt: I wish I had time to do both. Right now I really don't have time to do either. So I've been dabbling with forever just a little bit, but I'm anxious to... I haven't finished the Midnight storyline yet, I think. So I'm anxious to get back to that, too.

items.title: Red Rising Greenlit for Movie Adaptation With Author Pierce Brown to Produce
items.description: The Red Rising book series by author Pierce Brown has officially been greenlit for a movie adaptation from Paramount Pictures, with Hunger Games alum Francis Lawrence to direct.
items.author: Virginia Glaze
items.content:
The Red Rising book series by author Pierce Brown has officially been greenlit for a movie adaptation from Paramount Pictures, with Hunger Games alum Francis Lawrence to direct.

Red Rising is getting the Hollywood treatment more than a decade after it was first published in 2014. As confirmed by The Hollywood Reporter on October 16, Paramount Pictures has picked up the rights to the series, which will be brought to the screen by director Francis Lawrence.

Lawrence is known for his work on another young adult screen adaptation in the Hunger Games series, having directed every movie in the franchise sans the first one, which was directed by Gary Ross. Lawrence recently directed Stephen King adaptation The Long Walk, as well as the forthcoming Sunrise on the Reaping, the latest movie in the Hunger Games franchise.

Lawrence is also set to produce the Red Rising film alongside Cameron MacConomy for their about:blank production company, as well as Francesco Goedhuis and the author of the Red Rising saga himself, Pierce Brown.

Brown reacted to the news in a post on his Instagram account, writing, "Let fall the iron rain. Bloodydamn, I love this team."

Joining Red Rising is Justin Rhodes, who will write the movie’s script. Eagle-eyed IGN readers will recognize this name, as he is also involved in Netflix’s live-action Bioshock movie, which is reportedly still in early development. Rhodes is known for films like Terminator: Dark Fate, Traveler, and Liminal.

Red Rising is a sprawling book series that is planned to end with its seventh and final installment, which as yet has no release date. Set in a galaxy with a strict, color-coded caste system, the books follow Darrow, a Red — the lowest rank on the social totem pole. He and his fellow Reds toil tirelessly in the mines of Mars, with the hope that one day, they will be able to make the planet habitable for human life… but it turns out that this was already accomplished generations ago.

After learning of this massive betrayal, Darrow makes it his mission to infiltrate the highest social caste, the Golds, and set things right across the entire galaxy in a deadly conflict that spans more than a decade. If you're interested in getting into the books, you can check out our guide to navigating this sprawling adventure, which will no doubt come in handy once the movie eventually gets released.

This is the latest exciting news for book readers after Prime Video’s Fourth Wing series found its Xaden and Violet in actors Emilio Sakraya and Esther McGregor.

Image Credits: Penguin Random House, YouTube

items.title: James Gunn Shoots Down Milly Alcock Supergirl Rumors, Shares Man of Tomorrow Update
items.description: James Gunn has shot down rumors that Milly Alcock was fired as Supergirl and confirmed that he'll show Peter Safran an early cut of Man of Tomorrow later today.
items.author: Michael Cripe
items.content:
James Gunn has shot down rumors that Milly Alcock was fired as Supergirl and confirmed that he'll show Peter Safran an early cut of Man of Tomorrow later today.

The DC Studios co-chairman took to Threads on October 16 to dispel rumors surrounding his comic book movie projects. Although he's found putting a lid on the endless flow of internet rumors to be a little tiring, there were a few he wanted to take aim at when replying to a fan on Twitter/X.

First and foremost was the rumor that director Matt Reeves had completely departed The Batman Part 2 as director. Just about everyone now confirmed to be involved in the Elseworlds sequel had already clarified that Reeves would remain involved, so his denial is no surprise here. Another more recent rumor had some fans saying the star of Supergirl was let go, but that one's not true, either.

Milly Alcock has deleted all the posts related to Supergirl including her announcement one 🙃 https://t.co/FCHoI2lgOW

— Everything_DCU (@EverythingDCU_) October 15, 2026

DC movie watchers feared the worst for Alcock's character after noticing the star had wiped mentions of Kara Zor-El from her Instagram timeline. Although that's not completely true – some photos and Reels related to Supergirl are still very much publicly visible – her standalone film's trouble in theaters had some believing she would be leaving the DCU behind.

Gunn confirmed that's not the case, and it's easy to see why. Alcock first appeared as the character in 2025's Superman and reprised her role in Supergirl when it came out in June. She's been firmly established in the new comic book movie universe, but she's also poised for a triumphant return in Man of Tomorrow.

Earlier this summer, Gunn teased that Alcock was set to return as Kara when the Superman sequel premieres July 2027. He even went as far as to say that her dynamic with David Corenswet's Clark Kent would come into play in the new movie while filming was underway recently.

Speaking of Man of Tomorrow, the third rumor Gunn shot down had to do with whispers that the DCU film had received poor reviews after an early test screening allegedly featured a dark ending and the death of a beloved hero. It's another bit of gossip that the director and comic book movie executive confirmed "couldn't be more false," but it also came with an update.

It just so happens that Gunn had planned to show Safran a director's cut for Man of Tomorrow later today. He said his fellow DC Studios co-chairman will "obviously" be the first person to see any version of the film, adding, "and that's a month early!"

Gunn's words come at a time that has DC fans more anxious than ever. Superman started the live-action corner of the DCU off with a sonic boom when it swooped into theaters last year, but that momentum came to a halt with Supergirl. Although Lanterns helped reignite the fan base with strong casting choices and a grounded story, there's been some hesitancy amongst those online who fear films like Clayface and Man of Tomorrow won't deliver.

Gunn, at least, sounds more confident than ever. As far as rumors go, while fans await official updates, there's only so much he's willing to entertain.

"Oh brother," his post said. "You guys just have to stop listening to BS, and I'm mostly done shooting down rumors, as there are so many and I'm not on here much."

If you weren't aware, the former Marvel filmmaker has put rumors on blast before. When fans started to suspect Supernatural star Jenson Ackles would be playing the DCU's Batman, for example, Gunn quickly stepped in to put an end to things.

For more while we wait to see how the DCU is coming together behind the scenes, you can read IGN's interview with Safran, where we learned about a few casting updates for the new Mr. Miracle series. You can also read about what's next for John Cena's Peacemaker.

items.title: [UPDATE] Super Smash Bros. Player Mew2King Responds After Tournament Bans Him Over Bug Bite Concerns
items.description: Professional Super Smash Bros. player Jason 'Mew2King' Zimmerman has responded after his post about a bug infestation in his home resulted in him being banned from a competitive tournament.
items.author: Virginia Glaze
items.content:
UPDATE October 17, 2026, 9:30am PT: Professional Super Smash Bros. player Jason 'Mew2King' Zimmerman has responded after his post about a bug infestation in his home resulted in him being banned from a competitive tournament.

Mew2King took to X/Twitter to share a lengthy document regarding the online response to his post. The letter, which is more than 3,000 words long at the time of this update, saw the fighting game community member attempt to clarify a number of details surrounding his original, now-deleted post.

He said he lives with a caretaker, eight cats, and two dogs, and has only ever seen fleas in his home, which usually come from the cats. He also added that the viral photos of his leg were not captured recently and were instead actually from three months ago.

"I made some mistakes when posting out of frustration/venting that I regret," Mew2King said. "I mentioned that I get bit several times every week, but in the total year I was in Ohio it was very inconsistent as to when it happened, with some weeks (maybe months?) having nothing at all, and also some 2-3 day spans being bad (mostly several months ago). I don't have every exact timeline memorized for the whole year, but sometimes I misspeak and make mistakes or aren't always accurate but then realize later."

Made a post about my thoughts on things. Ngl im turning off replies cuz of the types of mean msgs many ppl sent me that i dont want to see or deal with. I wont be streaming or around for a while (maybe weeks idk). Thx for those who do care appreciate you

https://t.co/kJsNRn4jsz

— Jason Zimmerman (@MVG_Mew2King) October 17, 2026

ORIGINAL STORY: Professional Super Smash Bros. player Jason ‘Mew2King’ Zimmerman has been banned from a competitive tournament after posting photos of his concerning skin condition and complaining of a bug infestation in his home.

On the morning of October 16, 2026, Zimmerman found himself going viral due to a thread of posts he’d published on Twitter/X the day before. In the posts, he complained of suffering from swelling hands, which he attributed to either playing too much without rest or being bitten by bugs in his home.

“My hands are slightly swollen (could be from all the SSBM Fox or from the bugs in the house that bite me each day), like pink/red and puffy/fatter than usual, is there a way to fix this ASAP? I'm boarding my flight to Texas now,” he wrote.

He went on to share a photo of his hand and one of his right leg, which was covered in red, painful-looking bumps that appeared to be bug bites. Zimmerman claimed that these bites happen to him “every week,” and are a driving factor in his decision to move from Ohio to California.

“I had like a hundred of these on my body two months ago. Like, my entire body. This isn’t even nearly the worst picture, not even close,” he explained in another post. “It’s all bug bites from the house. Lived like that for all year. Or recent months.”

Needless to say, fans were fairly concerned about Zimmerman’s health and living conditions, with many theorizing that he was dealing with a bed bug infestation. Others urged him against getting on a plane or staying in a hotel, saying that he might spread the supposed bed bugs, which are known for sneaking into luggage and clothing to lay eggs at their next destination.

News of Zimmerman’s condition quickly spread online, prompting no end of discourse within the fighting game community — to the point where the tournament he was competing in, Xtreme Fighters Showdown, outright banned him from the event.

The tournament’s CEO published a statement about the situation on Twitter/X, alerting the public that Mew2King was no longer invited to take part in the competition as a direct result of his health issues.

“For the safety of our event, XFS 2026, we have politely informed Mew2King he will not be able to participate or attend our event this weekend due to a self-reported health concern,” the statement reads. “The health and wellbeing of our attendees is our priority. Thank you, and we’ll see you this weekend.”

Good evening, a message from our CEO, M333:

For the safety of our event, XFS 2026, we have politely informed Mew2King he will not able to participate or attend our event this weekend due to a self-reported health concern.

The health and wellbeing of our attendees is our priority.

Thank you, and we’ll see you this weekend.

— Xtreme Fighters Showdown (@xfshowdown) October 16, 2026

Zimmerman has not provided any public updates after this latest development, and has since deleted all the tweets discussing his skin condition.

This is the latest viral moment to make headlines within the competitive gaming space after pro DotA 2 player '23savage' was forced to play in front of police officers after one of his team’s training camps was raided by law enforcement.

And in September, Pokémon VGC regional champion Donghun Youm claimed that he lost a match due to his opponent's overwhelming stench, prompting a community-wide push for players to use deodorant at tournaments.

items.title: ‘There Should be a Game Award for Hot Dads’ — Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse Devs Are Fully Aware and Loving the ‘Horny’ Fanart for Their Game
items.description: The developers behind Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse are enthusiastic about the “horny” fanart they’ve seen of the game’s characters, saying they specifically made them "hot" to appeal to fans.
items.author: Virginia Glaze
items.content:
The developers behind Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse are enthusiastic about all the “horny” fanart they’ve seen of the game’s characters, saying they specifically made them "hot" to appeal to fans.

Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse released on October 15, and you’ve no doubt already seen the wealth of wild reactions to the title from players online — particularly in regards to its character designs.

Yes, it’s true; players are thirsty for Trevor Belmont and the various monsters they must fight as they navigate the chaotic streets of Paris, but they shouldn’t feel embarrassed about it. In fact, the devs were counting on this to happen.

Speaking with Fall Damage, marketing director and lead designer Bérenger Dupré and Sandro Bordier revealed that they are absolutely loving the thirsty reactions to the game’s characters — and that includes the “horny” fanart that they’ve seen on social media.

items.title: True Detective Season 5 Confirms Antonio Banderas and Nicolas Cage as Its Leads
items.description: True Detective Season 5 will officially star Antonio Banderas and Nicolas Cage as its two leads.
items.author: Michael Cripe
items.content:
True Detective Season 5 will officially star Antonio Banderas and Nicolas Cage as its two leads.

The next season of the HBO crime series confirmed the duo today with a video post on social media. Production is expected to begin in 2027, with a more specific release date for the follow-up episodes unclear for now.

True Detective Season 4: Night Country showrunner Issa López is back to serve as showrunner on Season 5. While most plot details remain under wraps this early in development, the next batch of episodes are expected to take place in Jamaica Bay, New York, with Banderas tapped as Rai García and Cage set as Henry Logan, as told by The Hollywood Reporter.

Banderas and Cage are two names that have circulated in the TV rumor mill for some time. Word of Cage's potential involvement surfaced all the way back in August of last year, but updates on that front then went quiet for months. It wasn't until this past weekend that the actor took the stage at New York Comic Con to tease that he was still in the mix.

"So, I think I’m probably going to do another season of television," he told the crowd (via THR). "I think I might do a season of True Detective. That’s OK that I’m the first to announce that, right?"

It wasn't too much of a surprise to hear Cage testing the waters, but confirmation of Banderas' involvement was mostly limited to the odd rumor and never felt quite as certain. Now, both are officially on board.

Cage. Banderas.

Season 5 of #TrueDetective starts production in 2027. https://t.co/tpTlnq0380

— True Detective (@TrueDetective) October 16, 2026

Cage made a name for himself with roles in movies like Raising Arizona, Face/Off, and National Treasure, but most recently appeared in projects like Spider-Noir, Longlegs, and Pig. Banderas' acting career has seen him star in things like The Mask of Zorro and Shrek, with his most recent roles including parts in Tony and Puss in Boots: The Last Wish. With previous seasons of True Detective led by unforgettable duos like Matthew McConaughey and Woody Harrelson (Season 1), and Jodie Foster and Kali Reis (Season 4), HBO is already off to a solid start.

For more, you can see how Cage took his NYCC appearance as an opportunity to speak out against AI. You can also see what IGN thought of Banderas' performance in this year's Anthony Bourdain biopic.

items.title: Pokémon Reveals New 'Holiday Helper’ Plush Collection With a Christmas Tree Pikachu and Clodsire Sled
items.author: Blythe Dujardin
items.content:
Pokémon has revealed a new collection of “Holiday Helper” plushies.

Pokémon shared an image of the new collection across the company's social accounts earlier today. The image shows five festive Pikachu plushies in varying sizes, including a Pikachu with a Clodsire sled.

A blog post on the official Japanese Pokémon website offers a closer look at the new plushies while confirming that the collection will be released in local Pokémon Center locations on October 24. North American Pokémon accounts only confirmed that the new plushies are “coming soon” to the U.S. via the Pokémon Center, which dropped the first wave of its 2026 holiday collection earlier this week.

Pokémon Reveals 'Holiday Helpers' Plush Collection Coming Soon to U.S.

The biggest plush in the image is a chunky Pikachu dressed in a full Christmas tree outfit, complete with a little star on his head.

The smaller Pikachu plushies, which additional images reveal are actually keychains, have the Electric type making various expressions in a Santa hat. A sleepy Pikachu holds a small cookie, a cutesy Pikachu is covered in snow, and a particularly mischievous Pikachu is riding a Porygon.

At a glance, it looks like Santa Clodsire is his own plush, but the Japanese Pokemon site shows the amphibious Pokémon connected to a small Pikachu riding a sled.

The announcement doesn’t include any information about sizing or pricing, but most plush keychains available on the Pokémon Center are between 4 to 8 inches tall The smaller guys look like they’ll be on the shorter end of that spectrum, which the Pokemon Center generally prices under $20.

The largest plushie's rounded shape is giving Squishmallow, and the Pokémon Center is generally home to the 12-inch Squish models. However, given how large he looks in the reveal image, the Christmas tree Pika could be up to 16 or even 20 inches tall.

The Pokémon Center prices Squishmallows at $29.99, though its self-developed larger plushies can reach up to $79.99. (Without getting into the multi-hundred-dollar life-size collections.)

It remains to be seen whether these Pikachus (and Clodsire) are the full collection of Holiday Helpers, or whether additional Pokémon will get the festive plushie treatment. The announcement also doesn't clarify whether the additional collection items shown in the Japan announcement, like Tangrowth holiday sweaters, will be exclusive to Japan.

The Pokémon Center is home to a ridiculous amount of Pokémon merch, including ongoing collections like the Holiday Village figure series and, of course, some of the best Pokémon plushies money can buy. Fans can look forward to new releases in these collections each holiday season, in addition to more general merch drops throughout the year.

items.title: Dragon Ball’s Goku Voice Actor 'Furious' Over AI Videos Using Her Voice Without Permission
items.description: Masako Nozawa, best known for voicing Goku in the Dragon Ball anime series, is slamming AI users for stealing her voice to create projects using the rapidly-advancing technology, calling it outright “theft.”
items.author: Virginia Glaze
items.content:
Masako Nozawa, best known for voicing Goku in the Dragon Ball anime series, is slamming AI users for stealing her voice to create projects using the rapidly advancing technology, calling it outright “theft.”

If you’re an anime fan, you’ve likely seen a few fan-made videos that use AI to copy characters’ voices, making them say some absolutely outrageous stuff. This trend isn't limited to English-speaking fanbases; it's also happening quite frequently in Japan, to the point where voice actors have gathered together to create the country’s first-ever guidelines regarding the use of AI voices.

Perhaps the most prominent of these actors is 89-year-old Nozawa. She’s a prolific voice actor who has been working in the space for decades and is best known as the voice of Goku (as well as Son Gohan and oodles of Goku variants) in Dragon Ball.

In an October 15 interview with Japanese outlet NHK, Nozawa was shown an AI video that used her voice — and her response to it was nothing short of scathing.

"That's not my voice,” she told the outlet. “I can't forgive them for using it without permission; it's like theft, and it makes me furious. I believe my voice and my acting are my own. If they're going to use even a little bit of it, they should get my permission.

"The AI-generated voice may resemble me. It may even be identical. But it lacks heart, doesn't it? Without heart, it's no good, no matter what the role. Even if it's just a crying voice, I believe it's different if you cry with emotion."

On September 30, the Tokyo District Court ruled that the unauthorized use of someone’s voice infringes upon their right to publicity in a landmark decision for both the voice acting industry and AI regulations as a whole. It’s one of Japan’s first major protections against AI, and it follows a lawsuit from famous voice actor Kenjiro Tsuda against TikTok over a video that used AI to imitate his voice.

"Rules are now being established, so I hope everyone will follow them. It's all based on the premise that everyone will truly follow the rules,” Nozawa said of this ruling.

Rather than relying on AI, Nozawa encourages fans to work hard to become voice actors themselves. "I want you to work hard so that you become someone people will definitely remember as a voice actor,” she said. “If you don't put your heart into it, you'll just be reading the lines, so make them come alive."

Nozawa is vice-chairperson for the Japan Actors Union, which held a press conference on October 15 to discuss its new guidelines regarding AI voices. "The progress of AI is amazing, isn't it?” Nozawa said in a statement. “It feels like the things I dreamed of as a child are becoming reality one after another, and it excites me. But it's disillusioning when it's being used without permission. I hope that everyone will follow the rules and we can create a future where both humans and AI can have fun together."

She isn’t the only prominent voice actor with something to say about AI; Toshi Shimada, best known for his role as Tomozo in the anime Chibi Maruko-chan, said that he “simply cannot accept the idea of ​​creating words I never said and songs I never sang, and then trying to monetize them. What I fear most is that the voice acting industry will collapse if unauthorized AI voices continue to be uploaded."

Michihiro Ikemizu, another prominent voice actor and Vice Chairman of the Union, explained that the “biggest problem is that people will lose their jobs. We want to build a track record with these guidelines and eventually aim for legislation."

This is the latest big news to come from AI voice acting after Amazon Prime Video caused a kerfuffle for introducing an AI-generated English dub of the anime Banana Fish back in 2025. The decision caused so much backlash that the streamer eventually removed it, but many fans felt that the fact it was included at all didn't bode well for the future of the dubbing industry.

items.title: PlayStation 6 Will Likely Have Sony's Own Take on Frame Generation, According to Latest Patent
items.description: Frame generation is established tech in games at this point, and we already knew that Sony was looking at the tecnology for the PlayStation 6, but the company has filed a new patent that gives a better idea of how it'll work.
items.author: Jacqueline Thomas
items.content:
Frame generation is established tech in games at this point. We already knew that Sony was looking at the tecnology for the PlayStation 6, but the company has filed a new patent that gives a better idea of how it'll work.

The patent, titled "Generation Super Sampling," (US-20260320740-A1), describes a mostly standard form of frame generation, where the model takes information from a traditionally rendered frame and then uses that information to generate an interpolated frame. The major difference is in how the model will be predicting how the frames will change.

DLSS frame generation works by taking rendered frames and then pulling motion vector information from the game engine. The suggested PlayStation model will also take input data from your controller to more accurately predict how you're going to be moving from frame to frame. The hope, according to the patent notes, is to limit the amount of latency or 'hitching' from frame to frame.

The patent also leaves the door open for multi-frame generation, which was introduced on PC with the RTX 5090 back in 2025. According to the patent notes, "In some embodiments, the predictions are not limited to an immediate next image in the image stream. The decoder system may be trained to predict any number of images before or after the input image."

It's hard to imagine why a console that'd presumably be attached to a TV needs to generate multiple frames, though. With PC gaming, multi-frame generation is only really useful when you're playing on a super-high refresh rate gaming monitor at 144Hz or higher. Even the TVs that do support high refresh rates are limited to 120Hz, which really limits the need for multi-frame generation. Still, having the option wouldn't be terrible.

My only concern with bringing frame generation to consoles is whether or not users will be able to turn it on or off at will. The nightmare scenario in my head is developers using it as a crutch, forcing it on to hit 30 or 60 fps in a game that'd otherwise be getting 15–20 fps. That kind of solution would introduce a ton of latency and visual artifacts, but then again, it's possible that taking user inputs into the frame gen pipeline could alleviate that issue.

Sony has been on a tear lately with its patents, and it really does seem like the company is building up to its next generation of consoles. Last month, it filed a patent that described an AI agent keeping an eye on your system and deploying fixes before you even notice a problem. Then, there was a patent that would implement an NFC reader into your PlayStation controller and would enable tap-to-pay. Because these are all only patents, there is a chance that none of these technologies see the light of day, but either way, the PlayStation 6 is turning out to be quite the interesting console to say the least.

items.title: Ghost of Yotei Sales Lag Behind Tsushima but Are Still Strong on PS5, Analyst Estimates Show
items.description: Ghost of Yōtei sales appear to be trailing behind Ghost of Tsushima, but that doesn't mean it's not still pulling big numbers on PlayStation 5.
items.author: Michael Cripe
items.content:
Ghost of Yōtei sales appear to be trailing behind Ghost of Tsushima, but that doesn't mean it's not still pulling big numbers on PlayStation 5.

That's according to Alinea Analytics head of marketing analysis Rhys Elliott, who shared data related to Sucker Punch Productions' 2025 sequel on X/Twitter. Although this is sales information that has yet to be confirmed by Sony, it may still give us a peek behind the curtain at how Ghost of Yōtei has fared on PS5.

The result: Sucker Punch's action follow-up has done well in its first year, even if it hasn't quite managed to pass up its predecessor. Alinea's analysis puts Ghost of Yōtei sales at about 5.4 million units, generating $407 million in revenue so far. Highlights from that update put the physical slice at a notable 36.8%, while PlayStation Store discounts remain largely few and far between.

Around 500,000 copies were sold in Q3 2026 alone. Alinea also reported that 50,000 players have picked up the digital Complete Edition – which comes with new content, including the recently released Echoes of Sekigahara expansion – in the two weeks since PlayStation launched it as a replacement for the digital base game. With the analysis estimating that around 6% of its existing base returned to play the new content, it seems Ghost of Yōtei is going strong – but there is more to the story.

Ghost of Tsushima, which launched in a market still coming to grips with pandemic lockdowns in July 2020, had generated about $418 million by the same point in its lifespan, Elliott added in a follow-up post. Factoring in Yōtei's base price of $70 vs Tsushima's base price of $60, as well as any discounts that followed, the latter is estimated to have sold almost 7 million copies by this point.

That puts Tsushima moving at a much faster pace in terms of raw units sold, but there is more at play here, especially considering revenue is almost neck and neck.

How do Ghost of Yotei’s revenues compare to Tsushima’s?

Our estimates (@alineaanalytics) show that Yotei has generated revenue of $407M. At this point, launch-aligned, Ghost of Tsushima had made $418M, so about 3% more.

As Yotei costs $70, and has had just two discounts, and Tsushima was $60 at launch (and was already discounted to $45 less than three months post-launch), Tsushima had sold more copies at this point. Nearly 7M versus Yotei’s 5.4M.

This is about 26% more revenue per buyer, which is consistent with PlayStation’s goal of extracting more revenue per player.

While that’s quite the gap in terms of copies, it’s worth noting that by this point in Tsushima’s lifecycle, there were about 117M PS4s and 10M PS5s in the wild, versus the nearly 100M PS5s currently out there right now (Yotei’s only platform).

That said, Yotei’s revenue is beginning to flatten more than Tsushima’s did, but perhaps the GTA-driven influx of new PS5s will soften that.

Yotei has proven to be an evergreen seller in a crowded market, shifting 1.8M copies this year ($121M in revenue) despite having just two small discounts and competing with what is one of the busiest and highest-quality release calendars … ever.

So yeah, anyone who says that Ghost of Yotei is a flop is flat-out wrong.

(Note: the Y-axis starts at $392M. Otherwise, the chart wouldn’t be readable, as the numbers are so close)

items.title: Nvidia App Update Will Let AI Agents Tune Your Graphics Card, but Some Users are Warning to Turn It Off
items.description: It's no secret that Nvidia loves its AI, and fresh off of launching RTX Spark – the new chipset for Agentic laptops – the Nvidia app now has a toggle that'll let AI agents control it. The problem is that it's turned on by default.
items.author: Jacqueline Thomas
items.content:
It's no secret that Nvidia loves its AI, and fresh off of launching RTX Spark – the new chipset for Agentic laptops – the Nvidia app now has a toggle that'll let AI agents control it. The problem is that it's turned on by default.

Nvidia added the option in Nvidia App 11.0.9.565 on October 13. In that update's patch notes, it says, "Nvidia App includes a local MCP server (Model Context Protocol) that lets a compatible AI agent control the Nvidia App using natural-language requests. This means your AI assistant like Hermes, OpenClaw or Perplexity can see your installed games and apply optimal settings, or enable Shadowplay to record gameplay, all through simple conversation."

It's not terribly surprising that Nvidia has added this option to the Nvidia app; after all, it did just debut its RTX Spark platform, which is built entirely around AI agents, so it makes sense that the Nvidia App would let users hook those agents in. But the setting isn't exclusive to RTX Spark systems and shows up for anyone who installs the latest version of the app.

And, of course, some people are upset and worried about the security implications of letting an AI agent control their graphics cards.

Silent Hill: Ascension cinematic director Agustin Cordes tweeted about the update, saying, "PSA: Can confirm that the Nvidia app is automatically updating and has *enabled by default* a setting which allows AI agents to control the app with very permissive rights. Besides the obnoxious privacy invasion and lame AI features, it's a high security risk you may not want."

Meanwhile, a swath of fans quoted his post, like user TheAcidBurns3, who says, "Please pay attention to this. You do NOT want your graphics card being accessed like this!"

User DATGUYCOOP, who appears to be a cybersecurity professional, urged most laypeople to turn the feature off, saying, "Just gonna say turn this feature off. Trust from the cyber security man. If you work with AI agents, its a good way to add filtering and protections and secondary checks, but to the common folk, it adds a threat vector that is better off closed. Now, there [are] no reported exploits as of yet, but it's new and adds possible connector that could mayhaps do something later, so just turn it off."

The problem really seems to be that the Nvidia App update turns the setting on by default, which is almost a surefire way to get people to hate any given feature in a tech product. Nvidia isn't new to letting AI systems and agents mess with your graphics card; after all, the company revealed Project G-Assist at Computex 2024, which was essentially an LLM that helped you manage GPU settings like clock speeds, fan curves, and more.

I've reached out to Nvidia about the security implications of this new Nvidia App update, and will update this article if a response is given. But regardless of what Team Green says, it's unlikely that this option is going anywhere any time soon. So, if you don't want your GPU driver to have a door open to AI agents, either install your graphics driver manually or turn off the setting by going into the Nvidia App, hit Settings, then scrolling down to 'AI Agents and App Connections' and disabling 'Allow Agents to control Nvidia App.'

items.title: James McAvoy Reveals He Once Pitched a Young Picard Star Trek Show
items.description: James McAvoy revealed he pitched a Picard Star Trek show that would have seen him yet again star as a young Patrick Stewart.
items.author: Michael Cripe
items.content:
James McAvoy revealed he pitched a Picard Star Trek show that would have seen him yet again star as a young Patrick Stewart.

The Split and X-Men actor opened up about his love for Stewart's time in the Star Trek universe during a conversation on Happy, Sad, Confused. He said it's something those overseeing the sci-fi franchise "nearly did," and although it never came to be, it's still an idea he's excited about to this day.

Instead of stemming directly from his love for Star Trek or even Stewart's Next Generation captain, Jean-Luc Picard, it sounds like McAvoy's idea for a limited series also came from his connection to Stewart himself.

"Mutiny on the Stargazer: That was a whole idea I had that I pitched the Star Trek people, as well. Nearly did it," the actor teased. When pressed for an explanation, he said, "I've got a whole story about an early Picard. I mean, all I really want to do in my career is play young versions of Patrick."

That, of course, is a reference to McAvoy's time spent playing Charles Xavier in films like X-Men: First Class, Days of Future Past, Apocalypse, and Dark Phoenix. It's a character made famous in the movie world by Stewart's aged-up portrayal in the original 2000s X-Men trilogy, and considering most seem to think McAvoy nailed the part in his follow-ups, a part as a young Picard could definitely make sense, too.

Alas, the Picard prequel never took off. The actor explained that he developed a whole story for what would have been a one-off season of TV that he still loves to this day, but for now, at least, his time as a young Stewart will be limited to the Marvel universe.

@happysadconfused #JamesMcAvoy shares details on the #STARTREK ♬ original sound - joshuahorowitz

"It was like a one-off standalone season when he took over as captain of the Stargazer, and what actually happened and the secret he's been holding his entire career," McAvoy said. "I just pitched it to them, talking to them, and they were well into it, but we had logistical issues, and we couldn't do it. But I love that story. I just go to bed and think about it at night."

Star Trek fans have already seen plenty from the life of Jean-Luc Picard. The character was first introduced as the captain of the USS Enterprise when he was played by Stewart in The Next Generation, but you don't have to be a die-hard fan of the franchise to know he's one of its most important characters. Despite this, the parts of his story we do know are mostly from later in his career, with his debut show – as well as projects like First Contact, Insurrection, and Nemesis – fleshing out the timeline further. The more focused follow-up series, Star Trek: Picard, premiered in 2020 and finished in 2023.

While McAvoy's story for a younger version of the character remains on the cutting room floor, you can check out what Stewart had to say about his hopes for a new movie. You can also read IGN's Picard Season 3 9/10 review.

items.title: VisionQuest Fans Think the MCU Show Is Hiding a Major Character Right Under Their Noses
items.description: VisionQuest watchers believe they've spotted another major MCU character in the new show's first episode.
items.author: Michael Cripe
items.content:
VisionQuest watchers believe they've spotted another major MCU character in the new show's first episode.

Paul Bettany reappeared as The Vision when his standalone Disney+ series premiered its first two episodes earlier this week. Although familiar Tony Stark-created AI bots like Jarvis (James D'Arcy), Edith (Emily Hampshire), and even Ultron (James Spader) are already keeping the hero company within his troubled mind, some fans believe VisionQuest has snuck in another big name from the WandaVision trilogy.

Warning! Potential spoilers for VisionQuest follow.

That character is none other than Wanda and Vision's magic-wielding son, Billy Maximoff, a.k.a. Wiccan. Played by Heartstopper actor Joe Locke in the 2024 Marvel show Agatha All Along, eagle-eyed viewers believe the character made his first appearance in the closing moments of the Vision show's first episode. If it really is him and it slipped by you, don't beat yourself up too hard; this is more of a blink-and-you'll-miss-it Easter Egg than an outright reveal.

After VisionQuest sets up White Vision's struggle with his identity, the first episode spends some time introducing another new face for a character we've already met. Wanda and Vision's other child, Tommy, seems to be alive after possessing the body of another human being (played by Ruaridh Mollica). Instead of materializing just outside of Westview like his brother, Billy, though, Tommy is living life in London as a pickpocket.

If fan suspicions are to be believed, Billy is well aware of his brother's location. After Tommy pulls off a small heist toward the end of Episode 1, one person with a familiar haircut can be seen walking amongst the crowd. Then, when Tommy meets up with his accomplice, Lisa (Lauren Morais), later down the road, that same person can be seen again, but this time, they're in a completely different position.

Could it be an extra out of place or a minor continuity error, or is it actually our first look at Wiccan's return as the WandaVision trilogy comes to an end? That's what fans are trying to figure out, but considering the MCU is known for tucking away the occasional visual Easter Egg and trick, many viewers wouldn't be surprised if this is our first hint at a family reunion.

The streets are saying Billy is following Tommy around… Oh, WandaVision-level delusions. WE ARE SO BACK! #VisionQuest https://t.co/BkdKXGHC2r

— alias (@itsjustanx) October 15, 2026

Wiccan's return is something fans have expected in the weeks leading up to VisionQuest's premiere. Aside from the fact that the show, which happens to be the last before Avengers: Doomsday marks the beginning of the end of the Multiverse Saga this December, offers an opportunity to reunite a powerful Marvel family, one recent trailer may also have contained another hint at Wiccan's return. The most damning evidence of his role in the show, however, is the fact that Mollica kind of let it slip that he and Locke had filmed some scenes together during an interview with Entertainment Tonight.

"It was amazing," Tommy's actor said of working with Locke on VisionQuest. "We actually shot our MCU stuff before we did the play [Clarkston], which was amazing. We met for a coffee beforehand to get to know each other, and we were just so excited. We became such good friends instantly, and then we did a play on the West End together and had this big secret that slowly started to leak as we were doing it."

Well, it all seems to be out there now, but we'll have to wait to see if the mysterious figure shown in Episode 1 really was Wiccan undercover. Until then, VisionQuest episodes will continue to roll out weekly. We'll get two episodes every week until the penultimate episode arrives November 3. The finale, Episode 8: "Forever," will then drop November 10.

For those who have yet to start VisionQuest, be sure to catch up on everything you need to know here. You can also see why Bettany thinks his Vision feels abandoned by the Avengers.

items.title: Apparent Leaked Footage Shows Canceled Assassin's Creed Game Set in Qin Dynasty China
items.description: Ubisoft was apparently making another Assassin’s Creed game set in ancient China, except this one was a full-fat AC with a massive open world and a fancy umbrella weapon.
items.author: Kirk McKeand
items.content:
Ubisoft was apparently making another Assassin’s Creed game set in ancient China, except this one was a full-fat AC with a massive open world and a fancy umbrella weapon. According to a new report, the game was called Assassin’s Creed Destiny.

Assassin’s Creed Jade will explore the same setting, targeting mobile. Destiny’s prototype footage appears to be aimed at modern consoles and PC instead.

Destiny was reportedly set during 206 BCE, where the Qin dynasty made way for the Han dynasty after a brutal civil war. The game likely would have focused on Liu Bang’s rise to power.

MP1st found the footage in developer portfolios. According to the report, the game was supposed to be a partnership between Ubisoft and Tencent, the Chinese conglomerate that owns huge portions of the games industry, including a 25% stake in Vantage Studios, a subsidiary that oversees some of Ubisoft’s biggest IPs.

The footage shows a hooded assassin battling through a siege headed up by warlord Xiang Yu, before switching to greybox testing environments for combat abilities. There’s a spinning umbrella weapon shown at one point.

Another snippet suggests players would have been able to choose between a male and female character, or it could have done the Shadows thing of having dual protagonists. Yin-yangs and ink brushes are used to tie the UI into the setting thematically.

While Destiny was seemingly cancelled, Assassin’s Creed Jade is still in development. The last we heard about it was that it was delayed to 2025. Considering it’s 2026 now, it’s probably safe to assume they’re having some issues getting the mobile game off the ground, which is ironic for a series about assassins who love rooftops.

Elsewhere in the world of hidden blades, leaps of faith, and stylish hoods, Assassin’s Creed Hexe is the next major game in the series. If leaks are to be believed, that’s got its own development issues, mind you. One report suggests Assassin’s Creed Hexe developers decided to rework the game, removing magical abilities from the mix.

Hexe's game director Benoit Richer recently departed the project for reasons unknown. That departure followed the exit of Clint Hocking, Hexe's creative director, sparking the beginning of a major internal reshuffle at the top of the franchise that saw Ubisoft veteran Jean Guesdon ascend to become Assassin's Creed Head of Content.

items.title: Elon Musk's Tesla Flying Car Reveal Met With Mix of Astonishment and Skepticism
items.description: Last night, Tesla CEO Elon Musk unveiled a car that he claims can fly, followed by a short demonstration of its ability to go airborne — and it's hard to think of a Tesla vehicle that's sparked more online reaction since the Cybertruck.
items.author: Jacqueline Thomas
items.content:
Last night, Tesla CEO Elon Musk unveiled a car that he claims can fly, followed by a short demonstration of its ability to go airborne — and it's hard to think of a Tesla vehicle that's sparked more online reaction since the Cybertruck.

The demonstration was held outside of a Texas SpaceX test facility, where Musk unveiled the car in front of a live audience. During that demonstration, Musk took to the stage, where he said, "We need an audience to prove it's not AI or SI, so you guys can tell people you saw it with your eyes," and that "you're going to see the results of what happens when you have a collaboration between the world's best car company and the world's best rocket company."

When the flying Roadster was revealed, it was remotely piloted to "make sure we don't kill anyone." The demo started off with the car facing a steep ramp, where it used suction to drive and park upside down, before eventually zooming up the ramp, jumping off, using rockets to right itself and land safely.

Turns out the future does have flying cars https://t.co/6fexPp6SXI

— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) October 16, 2026

The car uses thrusters from SpaceX in the rear of the vehicle and along the bottom to "basically fly like a rocket." Musk admitted this is "not necessarily a safety-optimized car," which is likely why, earlier in the event, he claimed that it would be "long-term the only manually driven car that Tesla makes." Musk added that this new Roadster would enter production in 2028, but with something like this, I'd expect a number of delays, if it ever makes it to the street at all.

Regardless, the car has been blowing people's minds. Christopher Lloyd, who famously played flying car driver Doc Brown in the Back to The Future movies, took to X / Twitter to say: "Finally...flying cars." Meanwhile, other folks, like user CARN0N tweeted out highlight reels of all the stunts that Tesla pulled off with the prototype rocket car. Some have even compared it to Rocket League.

Highlights of all four stunts Tesla showed off with the new Roadster today. https://t.co/chP6QEuVMk

— Oli (@CARN0N) October 16, 2026

"Rocket League is just a video game"

Tesla engineers: https://t.co/iPzBNywL4p

— Spawn Wave (@SpawnWaveMedia) October 16, 2026

There is a healthy dose of skepticism, of course. Tech influencer MKBHD tweeted out his disbelief, saying, "They really just got on stage and said this newly designed 4,000+ pound car can do flips and go half the speed of sound (380+mph) and will ship in 2028. This is a prank, right?"

NASA administrator Jared Isaacman was impressed, even if he was a bit skeptical, posting: "Hard to think of a wilder product unveiling. Not sure how quickly drivers are going to be leaping over each other in traffic, but damn, this was a cool way to introduce Roadster to the world."

Only time will tell if this new flying Roadster will ever actually see the light of day, or if it'll even be street legal in most places when it does. Musk sure seemed hopeful that Tesla would be able to get it out the door and into customer's hands in the next couple years, but really, we'll just have to wait and see.

items.title: 'We F***ed Up' — Wardogs Boss Admits Season 2 Hasn't Gone Particularly Well
items.description: Wardogs developer Bulkhead had some strong words to say about the rough launch of Season 2, admitting: "We f***ed up."
items.author: Kirk McKeand
items.content:
Wardogs developer Bulkhead had some strong words to say about the rough launch of Season 2, admitting: "We f***ed up."

Season 2 saw the introduction of XP and cash bonuses for people willing to play Blue Team, in an attempt to polish Lonestar’s tarnished reputation.

Unfortunately, the idea backfired as more experienced players quickly boosted their accounts on Blue. Usually it takes a while for players to unlock some of the deadliest gear, but the XP and cash boosts saw players quickly kitted out in the best armor and the most annoying weapons.

"We were wrong, we f***ed up," Bulkhead CEO Joe Brammer said. "This was an experiment — we thought we'd have this in for about a week.” The boosts have already been removed in a hotfix.

The cash and XP bonuses saw Blue Team go from the worst performing team to quickly dominating every match, attracting all the best players. The bonuses were 5% extra cash and 2.5% extra XP, but it was enough to attract the most try-hard players in the game.

"The only comment that annoyed me is when people say, 'They didn't address the core issues [with Blue Team]," Brammer continued, talking about team spawn placement. "Well, actually, we did rebalance the entire spawn setup for Bakurani, and we did test that out quite a lot and see that the difference had balanced out.

“We should have just stuck to our guns with that, really, but here we are — we tried, it didn't work, this is us holding our hands up."

Wardogs is still in Early Access so these kinds of teething issues are to be expected as the devs experiment and find the right balance for the 1.0 release. The game exploded in terms of sales, and the developers have been scrambling to keep up with its popularity since.

Bulkhead also had to contend with making sure Wardogs works on consoles, where the game will eventually land in 1.0. The developer already admitted to having to hold back Wardogs features to make sure it’ll run on Xbox Series S.

Wardogs Season 2 also introduced a new rain system that impacts gameplay. Players have to really cock their heads to pick up footsteps, and visibility for pilots is drastically reduced.
